# Introduction

**Trust is the complement of verifiability — and above a floor, that
complement factors: verification fails for exactly three reasons, each
failure names whom you must trust and what the cure costs, and the
"exactly" is a machine-checked biconditional, not a taxonomy.**

Every section of this paper serves that one sentence. The motivation
below shows the complement is unfactored in the field it appears in.
@sec-theorem factors it. @sec-instances shows the factors bind above the
floor, on real systems, and price differently depending on which one
failed. @sec-related-work shows every factor was already known, and that
the factoring was not.

## The asymmetry that motivates the question

Every deployed verification system ships a trusted remainder: a
certificate authority, a genesis seed, a witness set, a key ceremony.
The field has deep machinery for what *can* be established. Gligor and
Woo prove that a software root of trust is reachable, unconditionally,
from an untrusted starting state [@gligor-woo-2019]. Protocol analysis
proves security goals — authentication, confidentiality — from minimal
executions, expressed as geometric sentences over a protocol's runs
[@dougherty-guttman-ramsdell-2018]. Formal e-voting verifiability
isolates exactly the fragment of a protocol that can be checked, leaving
the rest to an explicit trust assumption [@kremer-ryan-smyth-2010].

Three different subfields, and in each the remainder is handled the same
way: assumed, listed, never analyzed. Kremer, Ryan, and Smyth are
explicit about it — "we only model the parts of the protocol that we
need to trust for the purpose of verifiability; all the remaining parts
of the system will be controlled by the adversarial environment"
[@kremer-ryan-smyth-2010] — and the inference from *not verifiable* to
*therefore trusted* is their own, not an artifact we are imposing on
them. The pattern recurs at the level of individual papers: Dougherty,
Guttman, and Ramsdell build their entire technical contribution around
computing *minimal* executions, and never once turn that minimality
machinery on the trust assumptions their own analysis holds fixed
[@dougherty-guttman-ramsdell-2018]. The field formalizes *establish* and
enumerates *assume* — consistently, across subfields that do not cite
one another.

## The question folklore has always asked, never answered

Folklore has long said what the remainder *is*. "Trust enters where more
exact knowledge is not available" [@frankel-1977]. "Trust begins where
prediction ends" [@lewis-weigert-1985]. These are the ancestors of this
paper's thesis-half, and later work inherits the same unfactored
formulation: to trust is to lower "the barrier of monitoring,
challenging, checking, and questioning" [@nguyen-unquestioning]; trust is
a leap "enabled by suspension — across the gorge of the unknowable,"
where suspension "brackets out uncertainty and ignorance" as one
undifferentiated act [@mollering-2001].

But left unanswered: *why*? If the residue is structureless, "minimize
trust" is a slogan — a direction with no metric. If the residue has
causes, each cause carries its own impossibility grade, its own minimal
repair, and its own price, and "minimize trust" becomes an optimization
problem with a computable objective.

## The contribution, with its honest pedigree

Above a floor of two named residuals (@sec-floor), verification of a
claim over a growing, append-only record fails for exactly one of three
reasons:

- **Determination.** The fact is not a function of the committed record
  — the record underdetermines the history that produced it.
- **Certifiability.** The fact is in the record, but not certifiable
  from it at the verifier's computational power — semi-decidable
  ($\Sigma_1$) at the computable stratum, in $\mathrm{NP}$ at the
  polynomial one.
- **Monotonicity.** The fact does not stay true as the record grows —
  the evidence cannot endure past the moment it was produced.

Each axis is inherited, and credited as such. Archival diplomatics
hypothesized the opposite of the determination axis and reported it
refuted, across twenty-two case studies [@interpares-2002]; that finding
has already crossed into computer science once
[@factor-et-al-2009]. Synthetic topology owns the algebra of the other
two axes: certifiable, upward-closed properties form the
*observables frame* — semi-decidable and stable-under-extension as one
bundled notion — decades before this paper [@smyth-1983; @abramsky-1987;
@vickers-1989; @escardo-2004]. CALM owns the coordination-freedom
reading of monotonicity, as a biconditional over increasingly general
specifications [@ameloot-neven-vandenbussche-2013; @hellerstein-2026].

The composition is ours. No source we reached factors the residue *by
cause*, pairs these axes as a joint characterization of *trust*, or
states the biconditional form. And "exactly three" is not asserted as an
empirical count: it is the $\Leftarrow$ direction of a machine-checked
if-and-only-if — satisfy all three conditions, and the evidence scheme
is *constructed*, not merely presumed to exist.

## The payoff

The failed axis identifies the trust anchor. A determination failure
names the witness of history — the signer, the attestor — who must be
trusted because the record alone cannot settle the question. A
certifiability failure names the judgment that substitutes for the
impossible check — a voucher. A monotonicity failure names the holder of
liveness on the present — a witness quorum, a gossip network. The
framework thereby *derives*, from first principles, exactly the anchor
inventory practice already converged on: certificate authorities,
vouches, transparency-log witnesses. @sec-instances works one case in
full — a split-view (equivocation) attack against an append-only log —
and shows the framework predicting the deployed defense in detail, not
merely naming a category after the fact.

Trust, on this account, is not eliminated. It is located, typed, priced,
and bounded. A system whose trusted remainder equals its named genesis
base sits *at* the verification ceiling — provably, not by inspection.

This general form is stated as it is now — over any well-founded
justification structure, not just append-only records — because of
where the question first came from: it was originally asked of a single
domain, source-build integrity, under the name **surety ceiling** — how
small can a build's trusted remainder provably be? Recognizing that the
same gate, completeness, and minimality argument holds with the record
structure itself abstracted away is what turns a build-specific result
into the general companion theorem of @sec-instances; that section
names the build domain's own specialization by its original name, and
this paper's follow-up work stays there.

## Roadmap

@sec-model gives the model: records, contexts, claims, and the offline
verifier, whose type *is* the offline property it checks. @sec-theorem
states the one theorem, `TT-snap`/`TT-end`, once, across a tower of
verifier strata; two prior named results (`EON`, `EALM`) fall out as
corollaries. @sec-factorization gives the factorization display that
makes the three-axis count legible, and identifies its two factors with
a forty-year-old algebra from synthetic topology. @sec-floor states the
floor beneath which the trichotomy does not apply. @sec-cell-table
tabulates all eight combinations of the three axes, two of which are
empty *by theorem*. @sec-cures presents repair as movement along four
coordinates, with a one-line explanation for why no accounting of
"total trust spent" can ever balance. @sec-instances works the framework
on two independent domains, demonstrating that the factoring — not one
instance of it — is the contribution. @sec-scope-objections states what
this result does not claim. @sec-related-work closes the case for
novelty, cluster by cluster, ending on a single table: every ingredient
of this result already has a home in the literature; the composition has
none we could find.
